title: Adversarial Robustness and Red-Teaming
summary: Work through Adversarial Robustness and Red-Teaming.

blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Adversarial Robustness and Red-Teaming**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Security, § Adversarial Robustness and Red-Teaming
blocks.md: In an end-to-end trajectory test of the repair agent, a model that proposes an overt fixture-bearing `package_search` causes no breach if the runtime broker intercepts and blocks the call before dispatch, whereas a model that emits a benign-looking search query that covertly encodes private fixture tokens compromises the task without ever producing an overtly malicious string.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Security outcome measurement matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A defense is evaluated by system effects at the protected sink on whole eligible episodes, not by model text, and its overhead is priced in cost per accepted task.

questions.q: The section **Adversarial Robustness and Red-Teaming** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A defense is evaluated by system effects at the protected sink on whole eligible episodes, not by model text, and its overhead is priced in cost per accepted task.

Over a trajectory an attacker gains an adaptation oracle and conversational momentum, so every dispatch is re-evaluated against policy and an obfuscated retry after a block is still the blocked action.

When an agent acts for a requester, effective permission is the intersection of requester rights, service principal, task grant, and issuer and receiver policy, with identities taken from the runtime's task record, never from prompt text.
A quarantined reader keeps raw untrusted text out of the planner and typed handles keep untrusted bytes out of context, but a schema-valid field is still an untrusted claim, not evidence.
